title: Learning What Not to Forget: Long-Horizon Agent Memory from a Few Kilobytes of Learning

paper.title: Learning What Not to Forget: Long-Horizon Agent Memory from a Few Kilobytes of Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Long-running language-model systems accumulate interaction history that outgrows the context window, so they must continually evict. When an eviction policy drops a load-bearing detail, for example an access token issued at login or a path the next call needs, the action fails. We present LRE (Learned Relevance Eviction), a few kilobytes, CPU-only, language-model-free scorer that learns which units of history are load-bearing and keeps them by verbatim extraction. Under a matched-budget comparison, in our experiment, no baseline dominates LRE on the accuracy-cost plane. On agents, LRE matches the accuracy of keeping the entire history overall. On the simplest tasks, it exceeds that no-eviction baseline by 27 % 27\% , while requiring zero compressor calls and reducing peak context size by up to 52 % 52\% . A controlled study trace shows LRE completes tasks where the others loop, finishing one such task in 37 % 37\% fewer calls than keeping everything and solving 14 14 tasks where no other run policy does. On conversational memory, LRE outranks dense and token-pruning encoders at zero neural cost. In downstream evaluation, LRE gives the best budgeted answer quality on LoCoMo reading 68 % 68\% fewer tokens. Its supervision can also be annotation-free: training only on the system’s own behavior recovers 95 % 95\% of the supervised scorer’s effectiveness. We argue that, because memory eviction in LLM agents is a fidelity problem, it requires a deployable proactive policy where the future query is unavailable and exact state is decisive, and that cheap learned relevance can be sufficient.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 2: Top (agent, AppWorld). Across a think/act/call/observe loop, a credential observed at step 3 and an identifier produced at step10 scroll far behind the budget cursor. LRE ranks them load-bearing and keeps them verbatim, so the login at step 17 succeeds. Bottom (conversation, LoCoMo conv). An identity fact stated at turn 5 of a 419 419 -turn, 19 19 -session history answers a question asked more than 400 400 turns later. LRE keeps that evidence turn. Large language models act as long-horizon agents and assistants that plan and act over extended interactions. A tool-using agent accumulates hundreds of action and observation steps, and a conversational assistant accumulates dialogue across dozens of sessions. In both cases the history outgrows the context window. The memory and compute cost of attention grows with context length, making long histories expensive to serve. Overly long contexts dilute relevant information, distract the model with stale detail, and degrade decision quality ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . The system must therefore evict : choose, within a token budget, the subset of history that preserves downstream quality. When eviction drops a load-bearing detail, the action fails even if the context is accurate. Eviction is different from retrieval, in a way that rules out the standard solution. A retriever runs at query time and conditions on the query ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Lewis et al., 2020 ) ; an eviction policy which runs at write time must decide what to keep before the query or action that needs it exists. The decision is proactive and query-blind, which excludes query-conditioned retrieval and explains why deployed systems fall back on reactive heuristics such as recency or decay ( Xiao et al., 2023 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ) . One way is calling a language model to compress history ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) which comes with non-deterministic behavior and paraphrasing challenges. Some methods learn what to retain rather than relying on heuristics ( Chung et al., 2024 ; Bui et al., 2025 ) , but score each unit with a forward pass or distilled gates tied to specific layers and heads, so retention still costs a neural evaluation and stays coupled to the host model. We argue the right primitive for eviction is a learned relevance estimate: cheap enough to run at every write, and faithful enough to keep verbatim what matters. We instantiate it as LRE (Learned Relevance Eviction), a scorer over cheap causal features that assigns each unit a keep-probability, retaining the highest-scoring units within budget via verbatim selection. The scorer can be trained on already logged data, on the order of a kilobyte (the agent scorer is 1.7 1.7 KB for our experiment), runs on CPU with no neural forward pass and no language-model call at compression time, and scores 1,181 1{,}181 units per second where a dense encoder manages 103 103 and an LLM token-pruner 36 36 ( 11.5 × 11.5\times and 32.8 × 32.8\times slower respectively; Table 13 ). On agents at a 2048 2048 -token budget, LRE completes tasks in 19 steps where the compressor loops to 49 ( Figure 1 ) and reaches 41.1 % 41.1\% task success against full history’s 44.0 % 44.0\% while needing zero compressor calls ( Table 2 ). On conversational memory the scorer ranks evidence at 0.829 0.829 macro-AUC on LoCoMo and 0.708 0.708 on LongMemEval S without ever seeing the question, above dense ( 0.643 0.643 ) and token-pruning ( 0.402 0.402 ) encoders that each spend a forward pass ( Table 3 ). A natural question is that supervision for “relevance” requires expensive annotation. We show it does not: a self-supervised label derived from the system’s own later behavior recovers about 95 % 95\% of the supervised model’s signal beyond random ordering ( Table 4 ). The signal a deployed system needs to learn proactive retention, is already present in its logs. We present: • LRE, a learned query-blind eviction policy. We present a few kilobytes, CPU-only, language-model call-free scorer method that learns which units of history are load-bearing and keeps them by verbatim extraction, with one design serving both conversational memory and long-horizon agents. • Pareto efficiency in both domains. Under matched budgets, LRE is an efficient and cheaper baseline that preserves or exceeds performance gains. On agent tasks, it matches the success rate achieved by retaining the entire history, while reducing context token size by as much as ∼ 52 % {\sim}52\% (details in Appendix H ); on conversational memory, in retaining useful content, it outranks dense encoders without a forward pass of its own ( Table 3 ). • Fidelity, not just retrieval, is what eviction needs. A controlled study traces LRE’s agent advantage to verbatim fidelity: extraction keeps the load-bearing context a task needs in the future while compression or recency loses them, leaving fourteen tasks that could be solved by LRE alone ( Section 5.2 ).

sections.heading: Memory architectures for conversational and agentic LLMs.
sections.text: LLM memory systems decide both what to write to long-term store and what to keep active. MemGPT ( Packer et al., 2023 ) borrows virtual-memory paging to move content between context and external storage, while MemoryBank ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) folds both decisions into a time-based exponential decay model. On the write side, prior works have organised history into episodes, reflections, or linked notes that are periodically consolidated ( Park et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Chhikara et al., 2025 ; Nan et al., 2025 ) , and event-centric variants decompose dialogue into propositions to keep recall non-lossy ( Zhou and Han, 2025 ) . These mechanisms improve what is stored, but retention within a tier defaults to recency, decay, or a further LLM call.

sections.heading: Reactive eviction under a fixed budget.
sections.text: A parallel line of work evicts directly from a size-capped buffer using cheap, query-blind signals. StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) retains a few initial attention-sink tokens alongside a recency window; H 2 O and SnapKV ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) keep the tokens that have received the most attention so far. They score a unit by how it has already been attended to rather than whether a later step may need it, and they operate on attention statistics at the token level inside a forward pass.

sections.heading: Learned retention.
sections.text: Recent work learns what to keep rather than relying on attention heuristics. Selection-p ( Chung et al., 2024 ) learns self-supervised, task-agnostic token retention, and TRIM-KV ( Bui et al., 2025 ) learns a per-token retention gate at creation time that decays over the trajectory and evicts under a budget. Both confirm that learned retention can beat hand-designed decay. Their signal is produced inside the model, by forward passes or distilled gates tied to specific layers and heads, so each unit still costs a neural evaluation. We address whether such predictive principle holds for content units at zero added inference cost, with a scorer external to and independent of the generating model.

sections.heading: LLM-based compression and its cost.
sections.text: At the expensive end, the model itself does the scoring. LLMLingua and LLMLingua-2 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) train a token classifier for compression rather than for any downstream task. In the agentic setting, context-management methods issue an LLM call to summarise or curate the accumulated history ( Kang et al., 2025 ) , adding latency on the critical path. Such summaries are typically conditioned on the current task, the query-aware advantage makes them a strong upper bound but not a deployable peer for a policy that can decide before the task context exists.

sections.heading: Related directions.
sections.text: Adjacent work studies proactive computation prediction ( Pan et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) , systems-level context management ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) , and annotation-free supervision ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ; Izacard et al., 2021 ) ; we discuss these connections further in Appendix A . Along the cost axis, prior work spans zero neural cost (recency, MemoryBank, StreamingLLM), one neural pass per unit (dense and lexical salience, H 2 O, SnapKV, Selection-p, TRIM-KV), and one or more LLM calls per decision (LLMLingua, ACON, AgentFold). Along deployability, it splits into query-blind and query-aware scoring, and along timing, into reactive and proactive eviction. We therefore bridge that gap with a learned , query-blind , extractive scorer that anticipates which past content a future query will need, at zero added inference cost and independent of the host model, evaluated on both agentic ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) and conversational ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Maharana et al., 2024 ) memory with downstream gains.

sections.heading: 4.1 Benchmarks
sections.text: We evaluate LRE on AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) , LoCoMo ( Maharana et al., 2024 ) , and LongMemEval S ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . AppWorld evaluates long-horizon agent execution under hidden-unit-test evaluation, while LoCoMo and LongMemEval S evaluate conversational memory retention under query-agnostic and multi-session settings respectively. Detailed benchmark descriptions, splits, labeling strategies, pseudocode and evaluation protocols are reported in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 4.2 Baseline taxonomy
sections.text: We compare against a range of memory retention baselines, including simple heuristics (Recency / FIFO and exponential decay MemoryBank Zhong et al. (2024) ), content-based scoring (TF-IDF centroid salience), and dense embedding similarity methods (frozen BGE encoder Xiao et al. (2024) ) and LLMLingua-2 Pan et al. (2024) . For agentic evaluation, we compare against a no-compression upper bound, FIFO (First-In-First-Out) retention, and ACON (in-fork) Kang et al. (2025) . ACON demonstrates competitive performance across a range of practical baselines; we therefore include ACON as a representative adaptive in-fork compression method for comparison under the agentic setting. For downstream performance evaluation on AppWorld, LoCoMo, and LongMemEval S , we use GPT-4.1-mini as the base model and GPT-4o as the judge model Hurst et al. (2024) . Baseline implementation details, along with pseudocodes are in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 5.1 LRE is Pareto-efficient on long-horizon agents
sections.text: LRE achieves task accuracy comparable with retaining full history while operating under a strict context budget ( Table 2 , Figure 5 ). On Easy tasks, it exceeds the unbounded baseline corresponding to a + 27 % +27\% relative gain over full-context setting, and remains competitive on Medium tasks where it outperforms both recency ( + 38.1 % +38.1\% ) and compression ( + 124 % +124\% ). This is achieved with zero compressor calls and with a peak prompt that is 25 % 25\% lower than full context on average, rising to a 35 % 35\% reduction under Hard settings ( 7.79 7.79 k vs. 11.95 11.95 k). FIFO keeps the budget but discards load-bearing state, so the agent loops, spending + 40 % +40\% more steps per task compared to LRE (30.6 vs. 21.8, and up to 33.5 for ACON). LLM-based compression retains salient content but incurs an inference overhead of 5.45 × 5.45\times model calls per task on average (rising to 7.37 7.37 on Hard) while yielding substantially lower task accuracy (if not optimized iteratively). sections.heading: 5.2 Why it works: load-bearing state survives under extraction
sections.text: The aggregate numbers leave open why extraction , specifically, is what helps. We isolate the mechanism on a single task (full logs in Appendix G ): a request to build a Spotify playlist from songs the user jotted in Simple Note. Because the task chains two apps, it hinges on several pieces of load-bearing state that must all be present when the playlist is assembled. Extractive LRE ranks the note-content turn and both login turns high and keeps them verbatim , so it creates the playlist with the exact token in hand and adds the songs, completing in 19 steps. Recency scrolls the note and the login state out of its window, so the agent re-fetches the note it already read and re-authenticates in a loop, running all the way to the cap without finishing. Abstractive compression preserves the plan but also summarizes by paraphrasing and likewise loops to the cap. LRE thus completes the task, finishes in 37 % 37\% fewer generation calls than the no-compression ( Figure 1 ). A further example is shown in Appendix F . The pattern holds in aggregate; fourteen of the test tasks are properly completed by LRE alone ( Table 11 , Table 10 ).

sections.heading: 5.4 Eviction preserves downstream answer quality
sections.text: Relevance ranking only matters if it improves the final task outcome. Figure 13 in appendix I evaluates each policy by feeding its retained context to the same QA model under a fixed 20 % 20\% retention budget. We see that more memory is not always better. On LongMemEval S , retaining the full context produces the worst downstream score (potentially a lost-in-the-middle effect Liu et al. (2024) ). LRE translates proactive relevance prediction into substantially better budgeted QA performance on LoCoMo. LRE-supervised achieves the strongest score among deployable policies while reducing context size ( 68 % 68\% fewer tokens than full context) ( Figure 13 , Table 12 ). sections.heading: 5.5 The supervision is already in the logs
sections.text: We further examine whether self-supervision for LRE is possible. We replace the human gold label with one the system can produce from its own behavior/log. The log-derived label recovers 95 % 95\% of the supervised scorer’s above-chance discrimination on LongMemEval S and 82 % 82\% on LoCoMo ( Table 4 ). We also report a negative transfer result. We also report an honest negative. In agents, a unit is labeled relevant when an identifier or entity it first introduces is later re-referenced by several subsequent units. Such reuse label does not transfer to dialogue, falling near chance on conversational benchmarks. The two domains therefore share a common principle, learning from what the system later used, rather than a single reusable label. The supervision needed for proactive retention is already present in the system’s logs.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented LRE, a learned relevance eviction policy that retains future-useful history through verbatim extraction with a small CPU scorer. Across both agentic and conversational memory settings, no evaluated baseline is simultaneously more accurate and cheaper. LRE approaches full-history performance under a fixed budget, requires no compressor calls or neural inference, and can be trained from the system’s own later behavior without annotation. These results suggest that cheap learned relevance is sufficient for proactive retention. A deployed system can learn what to keep from its own behavior, preserving load-bearing context without neural retention models or repeated language-model compression.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: LRE predicts future utility from signals available at write time. When future dependencies are weakly expressed or absent from the observed trajectory, the scorer can evict information that later becomes important. This limitation is inherent to proactive eviction and applies even with perfect training data. We evaluate on long-horizon agents and conversational memory, but not on multimodal memory, collaborative multi-agent systems, or environments with rapidly changing external state. Whether the same relevance signal transfers to these settings remains an open question. Additional discussion of evaluation, benchmark coverage, feature dependence, supervision choices, and deployment considerations appears in Appendix J .

sections.heading: Anticipating future need.
sections.text: The cost of mispredicting need is compute heavy: under recency or LRU, entries are discarded shortly before reuse and must be recomputed ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . This has motivated proactive systems. At the serving level, KVFlow and PBKV ( Pan et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) predict which agent or cache block will fire next from workflow structure and prefetch accordingly; at the agent level, AgentFold ( Ye et al., 2025 ) learns to fold and consolidate its own trajectory as it runs. These establish that anticipation beats reaction, but they anticipate computation from workflow graphs, or rewrite history through further LLM calls. We work along anticipating which past content an upcoming query will require, cheaply and without invoking an LLM.

sections.heading: Systems-level context management.
sections.text: KV systems such as PagedAttention ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) remove memory fragmentation and enable cross-request reuse, raising throughput. Such caching lowers the cost of re-processing a seen context, but doesn’t relieve the cost of attending to that context, which becomes error-prone once critical content is buried within a long window ( Liu et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Self-supervised relevance without labels.
sections.text: Training a scorer cheaply requires supervision that costs nothing to obtain. Hindsight relabeling ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ) reuses a failed trajectory by relabeling it with the goal it did reach for RL, and contrastive pretraining ( Izacard et al., 2021 ) learns dense retrievers with no relevance labels at all. We draw on this idea to derive retention labels directly from what later turns reused, at no annotation cost.

sections.heading: B.1 LoCoMo: Query-Agnostic Conversational Eviction
sections.text: LoCoMo Maharana et al. (2024) serves as the primary benchmark for evaluating query-agnostic relevance prediction in conversational context eviction. The dataset contains 5,882 dialogue turns across 10 conversations, where each conversation forms a distinct evaluation group. 1. Data structure. Each sample corresponds to a dialogue turn u i u_{i} , and all turns within a conversation form a group g ∈ { 1 , … , 10 } g\in\{1,\dots,10\} . The task is to assign a relevance score to each turn without conditioning on a specific downstream query. About 24% of dialogue turns are considered truly relevant (gold evidence across questions) 2. Label construction. We consider two labeling regimes. In the supervised setting, a turn is labeled positive ( y i = 1 y_{i}=1 ) if it appears in the gold evidence set of any question associated with its conversation. Because these labels are pooled across all the questions tied to the conversation, it yields a query-agnostic relevance signal. The model learns to identify turns that are generally load-bearing or informative for the conversation, rather than those that just match a specific query. In the self-supervised setting, a turn is labeled positive if it shares at least 40% token overlap with an eventual answer for training without explicit annotations. The choice of token overlap percentile is discussed in Section D.1 3. Splitting and leakage-free training. We use a Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) protocol over the 10 conversations. In each fold, one full conversation is held out for evaluation while the remaining nine are used for training. To prevent information leakage, the vectorizer and StandardScaler are fitted strictly on training data within each fold. A deduplication guard removes any exact-text overlaps between training and test folds. In LoCoMo, this has minimal effect, removing only 8 training instances corresponding to 3 generic utterances (e.g., “Bye!”, “Take care!”). 4. Feature representation and scoring. Each unit is mapped to a feature vector combining: (i) a TF-IDF representation of the text, and (ii) six trajectory features: position, recency, length, digit count, question-marker presence, and capitalized-word count ( Table 6 ). A logistic regression model is trained to estimate relevance scores p i = P ⁡ ( y i = 1 ∣ u i ) p_{i}=P(y_{i}=1\mid u_{i}) using these features. At inference time, the model scores all units in the held-out conversation without access to downstream queries. 5. Evaluation and downstream usage. The model is evaluated both intrinsically and extrinsically. For intrinsic evaluation, we compute ROC-AUC over held-out folds ( Appendix E ). For extrinsic evaluation, retained dialogue turns are passed verbatim into a downstream QA model. Performance is measured using token-level F1, as suggested by Maharana et al. sections.heading: B.2 LongMemEval S : Scalable Session-Level Eviction
sections.text: LongMemEval S Wu et al. (2024) evaluates session-level context eviction under large-scale, query-dependent retrieval settings. Unlike LoCoMo, which operates over dialogue turns, LongMemEval S defines each eviction unit as a full session within a question-specific haystack. 1. Data structure and eviction units. The dataset (longmemeval_s) contains up to 500 questions, where each question defines an independent group. Each group consists of approximately 50 sessions forming a retrieval haystack. The task is highly sparse, with only 5% of sessions are actually relevant per question (much more sparse / harder retrieval problem). 2. Label construction. In the supervised setting, a session is labeled positive ( y i = 1 y_{i}=1 ) if its session ID appears in the question-specific answer_session_ids . In the self-supervised setting, a proxy label is assigned if the session contains at least 40% token overlap with the eventual answer for evaluating training performance without annotations ( Section D.1 ). 3. Splitting and leakage prevention. We use grouped K-fold cross-validation with k = 5 k=5 due to the high computational cost of full leave-one-group-out evaluation over 500 questions. A critical challenge in LongMemEval S is cross-question session reuse. To address this, we apply a deduplication guard that removes any training session whose exact text appears in the held-out question’s haystack. This eliminates over 51,000 duplicate training instances and prevents memorization-based leakage. 4. Feature representation and scoring. Each session is represented using a fusion of: (i) TF-IDF lexical features, and (ii) six standardized trajectory features. A logistic regression model outputs relevance scores p i = P ⁡ ( y i = 1 ∣ u i ) p_{i}=P(y_{i}=1\mid u_{i}) without access to the downstream question context. 5. Evaluation protocol. LongMemEval S is evaluated on both retrieval quality and downstream task performance.For relevance prediction, we compute ROC-AUC. sections.heading: B.3 AppWorld: Agentic Long-Horizon Evaluation
sections.text: AppWorld is a long-horizon tool-use benchmark in which an agent writes Python against application APIs (Venmo, Spotify, Gmail, and others) to complete a natural-language task, graded by hidden unit tests. We evaluate on the test_normal split (168 tasks: 57 Easy, 48 Medium, 63 Hard), following Kang et al. (2025) and train the agent scorer on the 90 tasks of the disjoint train split. The agent and, where applicable, the compressor are gpt-4.1-mini. 1. Trajectory generation and training data. We first execute an unevicted baseline agent ("nocomp") on the AppWorld training split consisting of 90 tasks. This produces full execution trajectories containing interleaved Python code actions and environment observations, which are used as training data for the LRE scorer. 2. Self-supervised labeling via quotation reuse. Since no human relevance annotations are available, we construct a zero-supervision label using a hindsight reuse criterion. Let z i z_{i} denote an identifier introduced at step i i . The label is defined as: • y i = 1 y_{i}=1 if z i z_{i} is reused in at least 3 subsequent steps, • otherwise y i = 0 y_{i}=0 . This identifies load-bearing identifiers that persist across the execution trajectory. 3. Scorer training. The logistic regression scorer ( s 90 s_{90} ) is evaluated under a Leave-One-Task-Out (LOGO) protocol. 4. Inference and eviction loop. During evaluation on test task splits, the agent operates in a ReAct-style loop. When the context length exceeds the token budget ( B = 2048 B=2048 ), the eviction module is triggered. LRE performs CPU-based scoring of historical units. Units are ranked by score-per-token and retained greedily. This ensures chronological and verbatim reconstruction of the compressed context and preserves exact API identifiers and execution-relevant symbols. 5. Evaluation and Task Goal Completion (TGC). AppWorld evaluates success using Task Goal Completion (TGC), computed via hidden unit tests that operate on the final environment state. A known failure mode is self-reported success bias , where task success is determined from the agent’s own completion signal rather than from the environment state. This is problematic because the agent can declare success without having actually produced a state that satisfies the underlying task constraints, leading to an empirical inflation of success rates by approximately 2 × 2\times ( table 5 ). sections.heading: LRE variants.
sections.text: All three share one model (an L2 logistic regression with balanced class weights, vectorizer and scaler fit per fold on training units only) and the inference s i = P ⁡ ( relevant ∣ u i ) s_{i}=P(\mathrm{relevant}\mid u_{i}) with no neural pass. They differ only in label and features: • LRE-supervised . Label: human gold evidence already given in the benchamark. • LRE-self-sup (zero-annotation). Label: the response-overlap proxy (a turn is positive if its content tokens cover ≥ 0.4 \geq 0.4 of some eventual answer’s), derived from later responses with no annotation needed. Section D.1 shows the justification for the choice of token coverage value. • LRE-content (ablation). Label: human gold evidence (same as LRE-supervised). Features: the TF-IDF text vector alone , with the six trajectory features removed. This isolates the contribution of the trajectory block: the gap between LRE-supervised and LRE-content on a given dataset is what those six features add over text-only scoring.

sections.heading: Appendix D Justification of Self-Supervised Label Design Choices
sections.text: We evaluate label quality using two quantities: (i) AUC-vs-gold , which measures how well self-supervised labels align with human-annotated gold relevance labels (higher is better; 0.5 corresponds to random alignment), and (ii) positive rate , which denotes the fraction of units labeled as positive under a given rule. For agentic settings, we additionally report LOTO AUC (Leave-One-Task-Out AUC), which measures how well a classifier trained on these labels generalizes to unseen tasks.

sections.heading: D.1 Conversational Overlap Threshold ( τ = 0.4 \tau=0.4 )
sections.text: For conversational self-supervision, a turn is labeled positive if its content overlaps with a downstream response above a threshold τ \tau . We select τ = 0.4 \tau=0.4 based on a joint sweep across LoCoMo and LongMemEval S , evaluating AUC-vs-gold and label sparsity. Table 7 summarizes the results. τ \tau LoCoMo AUC LongMemEval S AUC LoCoMo + LongMemEval S + 0.2 0.742 0.647 0.94 0.47 0.3 0.754 0.686 0.85 0.38 0.4 0.769 0.698 0.66 0.29 0.5 0.764 0.682 0.61 0.22 0.6 0.758 0.679 0.39 0.13 0.8 0.754 0.652 0.30 0.11 Table 7: Sweep over response-overlap threshold τ \tau . Why τ = 0.4 \tau=0.4 is chosen: First, it is the joint maximizer of AUC-vs-gold across both datasets. Second, it lies in a flat optimum region ( τ ∈ [ 0.3 , 0.5 ] \tau\in[0.3,0.5] ), where performance varies by at most 0.016 0.016 AUC. This indicates stability. Why not other values: Lower thresholds ( τ = 0.2 , 0.3 \tau=0.2,0.3 ) produce excessively high positive rates on LoCoMo ( 0.85 0.85 – 0.94 0.94 ). This collapses the ranking problem into near-uniform positives and weakens discrimination. Such a near-degenerate label distribution does not reflect real-world deployment nuances. Higher thresholds ( τ ≥ 0.5 \tau\geq 0.5 ) reduce coverage too aggressively (down to 0.11 0.11 – 0.61 0.61 positive rate) and degrade alignment with gold annotations.

sections.heading: D.2 Agentic Reuse Breadth ( b = 3 b=3 )
sections.text: For agentic trajectories, a step is labeled positive if an identifier it introduces is reused at least b b times in subsequent steps. We evaluate b ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } b\in\{1,2,3,4,5\} using Leave-One-Task-Out evaluation. b b Pos-rate # Positives LOTO AUC 1 0.811 1269 0.878 2 0.582 911 0.830 3 0.432 676 0.828 4 0.335 524 0.835 5 0.271 424 0.847 Table 8: Sweep over reuse breadth b b for agentic self-supervision. LOTO AUC (Leave-One-Task-Out Area Under the ROC Curve) measures how well a classifier trained on these labels ranks truly relevant steps above irrelevant ones in unseen tasks. A value of 0.5 corresponds to random ranking, while 1.0 corresponds to perfect separation. Why b = 3 b=3 is chosen: Unlike the conversational case, LOTO AUC is relatively flat across all values ( 0.83 0.83 – 0.88 0.88 ). We therefore select b = 3 b=3 based on semantic and operational criteria. First, b = 1 b=1 is overly permissive, marking 81% of steps as positive. This collapses the eviction task into a near-majority-class problem, where ranking becomes dominated by trivial structural correlations rather than load-bearing utility. Second, b = 3 b=3 yields a moderate positive rate ( ≈ 0.43 \approx 0.43 ), which aligns with the expected compression domain Kang et al. (2025) in which only a subset of trajectory state can be retained. Why not other values: Values b ≥ 4 b\geq 4 become too selective, reducing the positive set to 27 27 – 34 % 34\% , which harms coverage of reusable context. b ≤ 2 b\leq 2 over-labels transient identifiers that are only briefly reused. We choose a parameter value that reflects real deployment nuances and therefore fix b = 3 b=3 , a semantic choice that captures repeatedly-reused, load-bearing state while maintaining a stable and informative training signal.

sections.heading: Appendix E Metrics: definitions and recovery
sections.text: This appendix defines every reported score in both domains, then describes how the agent metric and its costs are recovered honestly.

sections.heading: ROC-AUC (per group).
sections.text: Each method assigns a real-valued keep-score s i s_{i} to every unit u i u_{i} of a group, scored against the binary gold label y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i}\in\{0,1\} . Let 𝒫 = { i : y i = 1 } \mathcal{P}=\{i:y_{i}{=}1\} and 𝒩 = { i : y i = 0 } \mathcal{N}=\{i:y_{i}{=}0\} be the relevant and irrelevant units, with P = | 𝒫 | P=|\mathcal{P}| , N = | 𝒩 | N=|\mathcal{N}| . The area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve equals the probability that a random relevant unit outscores a random irrelevant one, computed exactly as the normalized Mann–Whitney statistic Mann and Whitney (1947) AUC = 1 P ​ N ∑ i ∈ 𝒫 ∑ j ∈ 𝒩 ( 𝟏 [ s i > s j ] + 1 2 1 [ s i = s j ] ) . \mathrm{AUC}\;=\;\frac{1}{P\,N}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}}\Big(\mathbf{1}[\,s_{i}>s_{j}\,]+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}[\,s_{i}=s_{j}\,]\Big). AUC = 1 \mathrm{AUC}=1 is a perfect ranking (every relevant unit above every irrelevant one), 0.5 0.5 is chance (random ordering), and a value < 0.5 <0.5 means the score is anti -correlated with relevance. AUC is threshold-free and invariant to the positive rate, so it measures the ranking quality an eviction policy needs (what to keep first) without committing to a budget. A group is scored only if it contains at least one relevant and one irrelevant unit (otherwise AUC is undefined).

sections.heading: Macro-AUC.
sections.text: The per-group AUCs are averaged with equal weight, macro-AUC = 1 | G | ​ ∑ g ∈ G AUC g \text{macro-AUC}=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\mathrm{AUC}_{g} , so a large group cannot dominate a small one; the groups are conversations on LoCoMo and questions on LongMemEval S .

sections.heading: Recall@budget.
sections.text: A retention policy keeps the K = ⌈ b ​ n ⌉ K=\lceil b\,n\rceil highest-scoring of the n n units at budget fraction b ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.4 } b\in\{0.1,0.2,0.4\} . Recall@ b = | kept ∩ 𝒫 | / P b=|\text{kept}\cap\mathcal{P}|/P is the fraction of relevant units that survive, averaged over groups.

sections.heading: Budget@recall (iso-accuracy efficiency).
sections.text: The inverse statistic: the smallest budget fraction b b at which recall@ b b reaches a target (e.g. 0.8 0.8 ), averaged over groups, reported as the saving relative to recency at the same recall.

sections.heading: Token-F1 (LoCoMo).
sections.text: With the answerer reading only the retained context, we compare its answer A A to the gold answer G G as bags of normalized content tokens. With prec = | A ∩ G | / | A | \mathrm{prec}=|A\cap G|/|A| and rec = | A ∩ G | / | G | \mathrm{rec}=|A\cap G|/|G| , token-F1 = 2 ​ prec ⋅ rec prec + rec , \text{token-F1}=\frac{2\,\mathrm{prec}\cdot\mathrm{rec}}{\mathrm{prec}+\mathrm{rec}}, the standard extractive-QA overlap, averaged over questions.

sections.heading: LLM-judge (LongMemEval S ).
sections.text: Free-form answers are graded by a model stronger than the answerer (gpt-4o judging gpt-4.1-mini, to avoid self-grading): the judge sees the question, the gold answer, and the candidate, and returns a binary correct/incorrect vote; the score is the fraction judged correct. The judge was validated on crafted correct, wrong, and paraphrase cases.

sections.heading: Throughput, neural calls, dollar cost.
sections.text: Units per second is the measured rate at which a loaded scorer scores resident units (hardware recorded). Neural forward passes per unit counts the encoder or classifier passes a method performs per scored unit.

sections.heading: Task Goal Completion (TGC).
sections.text: The all-or-nothing success metric on AppWorld: a task scores 1 1 only if every hidden unit test passes (partial credit such as 3 3 of 4 4 tests counts as 0 0 ), and TGC % \text{TGC}\% over a difficulty bucket is the mean over its tasks. How we recover true TGC (rather than the inflated self-report) is in § E.5 .

sections.heading: Cost axes.
sections.text: cLLM is compressor language-model calls per task (the number of compression events). Input tokens per request (in/req) is the mean prompt size per generation, our peak-token proxy since the true per-step peak is not logged. Total tokens per task sums agent and recovered compressor tokens.

sections.heading: Recovering true TGC by replay.
sections.text: The agent framework ships with its environment evaluation disabled, so the run’s self-reported completion flag overstates success and is not Task Goal Completion. We recover true TGC at zero model cost: because a freshly constructed environment resets task state, we replay each task’s logged action sequence into a fresh environment and then call the environment’s evaluation, which passes only when all hidden unit tests pass. The replay reconstructs the final state deterministically rather than reporting the empty-environment artifact. All reported TGC values use this recovered metric, never the self-report. Algorithm 12 gives the procedure. 1: Task id T T , logged action sequence (the agent’s code blocks) 2: world ← AppWorld ​ ( T ) \mathrm{world}\leftarrow\textsc{AppWorld}(T) ⊳ \triangleright fresh env: resets to T T ’s initial state 3: for each action \mathrm{action} in the logged sequence do 4: world . execute ⁡ ( clean ​ _ ​ code ​ ( action ) ) \mathrm{world}.\mathrm{execute}\big(\mathrm{clean\_code}(\mathrm{action})\big) ⊳ \triangleright replay to rebuild final state; errors swallowed 5: end for 6: r ← world . evaluate ⁡ ( ) r\leftarrow\mathrm{world}.\mathrm{evaluate}() ⊳ \triangleright run hidden unit tests on the reconstructed state 7: tgc ← ( r . num _ passes = r . num _ tests ) ∧ ( r . num _ failures = 0 ) \mathrm{tgc}\leftarrow\big(r.\mathrm{num\_passes}=r.\mathrm{num\_tests}\big)\wedge\big(r.\mathrm{num\_failures}=0\big) ⊳ \triangleright all-or-nothing 8: return tgc \mathrm{tgc} ⊳ \triangleright written to tgc.json ; never the agent self-report Figure 12: Recovery of true TGC by replay ($0, no LLM call): replay_eval.py . A fresh environment resets to the initial state, so we replay the logged actions to reconstruct the agent’s final state before evaluating.

sections.heading: Appendix J Extended limitations
sections.text: This appendix expands the limitations stated in the main text. We group them by scope: evaluation, method, supervision, measurement, and generalization. Each limitation lists what we did to mitigate it and, where relevant, what a deployment would need to verify before relying on LRE.

sections.heading: Single-seed agent comparison.
sections.text: The AppWorld results are reported at one seed ( s1 ). The host agent (gpt-4.1-mini) is non-deterministic, so per-task outcomes carry run-to-run noise that a single seed cannot characterize.

sections.heading: In-fork ACON baseline.
sections.text: ACON’s published fork ships the unoptimized compression prompt and we used it as it is. The fair comparison that licenses our claim is the matched in-fork one (identical agent, identical seed, identical evaluation harness).

sections.heading: Benchmark coverage.
sections.text: We evaluate on three benchmarks: LoCoMo and LongMemEval S for conversational memory, AppWorld for long-horizon agents. These cover dialogue and tool-use coding agents but do not include web-browsing agents, multimodal agents, or open-domain coding agents (e.g., SWE-bench). The Pareto-efficiency claim is supported within these regimes.

sections.heading: Subset of AppWorld used.
sections.text: We evaluate on test_normal (168 tasks). We do not evaluate on test_challenge (417 tasks).

sections.heading: Budget-bounded performance.
sections.text: On tasks whose required state exceeds the operating budget (AppWorld Hard at B = 2048 B=2048 being the clearest case) no-compression wins because retaining everything is the only way to keep state that does not fit. LRE therefore complements, rather than replaces, unbounded retention when the deployment can afford it. The right deployment question is whether the budget is binding; where it is, LRE is Pareto-efficient.

sections.heading: Eviction unit granularity.
sections.text: Our agent unit is the (action, observation) pair; our conversational unit is the dialogue turn or session. We do not evict at the token level inside a single forward pass, which is what KV-cache methods such as H 2 O ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , SnapKV ( Li et al., 2024 ) , Selection-p ( Chung et al., 2024 ) , and TRIM-KV ( Bui et al., 2025 ) do. Token-level methods are complementary: they operate inside the model and require model-internal signals; LRE operates outside the model and requires only logged behavior. A deployment could plausibly combine them (LRE for unit-level retention, token pruning inside each retained unit), but we do not evaluate that combination here.

sections.heading: Host-model coupling of training data.
sections.text: We do not test transfer to other host models (different tokenizers, different action styles, different failure modes). The scorer is small enough to retrain per host model in minutes from logged behavior, so the limitation is operational rather than fundamental, but a deployment switching host models should retrain.

sections.heading: Feature-set dependence.
sections.text: The learned scorer operates on a compact set of causal features that we designed to be inexpensive, model-agnostic, and available at decision time. While these features transfer across the benchmarks studied here, we do not claim that they are universally optimal. Different deployments may expose different signals, interaction patterns, memory units, or notions of future utility. In practice, a production system should treat our feature set as a reference implementation rather than a fixed specification, and should measure and validate its own candidate features from logged behavior before deployment. The broader claim of LRE is that future utility can be learned from causal signals available at write time, not that any particular feature set is universally sufficient.

sections.heading: Fixed self-supervised threshold.
sections.text: The conversational self-supervised label uses a fixed answer-recall threshold of τ = 0.4 \tau=0.4 , jointly optimal on LoCoMo and LongMemEval S . In deployment, however, the right rule is to set τ \tau implicitly (through a target positive rate on a sample of logged exchanges) rather than to inherit our value. The τ = 0.4 \tau=0.4 choice is justified empirically (Table 7 ); we do not claim it is universal.

sections.heading: No multimodal or extended unit types.
sections.text: The eviction unit is text. Multimodal agents whose load-bearing state includes images, audio, or large code blobs would require the unit representation and the token-cost function to be extended; we have not done so.

When an eviction policy drops a load-bearing detail, for example an access token issued at login or a path the next call needs, the action fails. We present LRE (Learned Relevance Eviction), a few kilobytes, CPU-only, language-model-free scorer that learns which units of history are load-bearing and keeps them by verbatim extraction. Under a matched-budget comparison, in our experiment, no baseline dominates LRE on the accuracy-cost plane. On agents, LRE matches the accuracy of keeping the entire history overall. On the simplest tasks, it exceeds that no-eviction baseline by 27 % 27\% , while requiring zero compressor calls and reducing peak context size by up to 52 % 52\% . A controlled study trace shows LRE completes tasks where the others loop, finishing one such task in 37 % 37\% fewer calls than keeping everything and solving 14 14 tasks where no other run policy does. On conversational memory, LRE outranks dense and token-pruning encoders at zero neural cost. In downstream evaluation, LRE gives the best budgeted answer quality on LoCoMo reading 68 % 68\% fewer tokens. Its supervision can also be annotation-free: training only on the system’s own behavior recovers 95 % 95\% of the supervised scorer’s effectiveness. We argue that, because memory eviction in LLM agents is a fidelity problem, it requires a deployable proactive policy where the future query is unavailable and exact state is decisive, and that cheap learned relevance can be sufficient. Large language models act as long-horizon agents and assistants that plan and act over extended interactions. A tool-using agent accumulates hundreds of action and observation steps, and a conversational assistant accumulates dialogue across dozens of sessions. In both cases the history outgrows the context window. The memory and compute cost of attention grows with context length, making long histories expensive to serve. Overly long contexts dilute relevant information, distract the model with stale detail, and degrade decision quality ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . The system must therefore evict : choose, within a token budget, the subset of history that preserves downstream quality. When eviction drops a load-bearing detail, the action fails even if the context is accurate. Eviction is different from retrieval, in a way that rules out the standard solution. A retriever runs at query time and conditions on the query ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ; Lewis et al., 2020 ) ; an eviction policy which runs at write time must decide what to keep before the query or action that needs it exists. The decision is proactive and query-blind, which excludes query-conditioned retrieval and explains why deployed systems fall back on reactive heuristics such as recency or decay ( Xiao et al., 2023 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ) . One way is calling a language model to compress history ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Kang et al., 2025 ) which comes with non-deterministic behavior and paraphrasing challenges. Some methods learn what to retain rather than relying on heuristics ( Chung et al., 2024 ; Bui et al., 2025 ) , but score each unit with a forward pass or distilled gates tied to specific layers and heads, so retention still costs a neural evaluation and stays coupled to the host model. We argue the right primitive for eviction is a learned relevance estimate: cheap enough to run at every write, and faithful enough to keep verbatim what matters. We instantiate it as LRE (Learned Relevance Eviction), a scorer over cheap causal features that assigns each unit a keep-probability, retaining the highest-scoring units within budget via verbatim selection. The scorer can be trained on already logged data, on the order of a kilobyte (the agent scorer is 1.7 1.7 KB for our experiment), runs on CPU with no neural forward pass and no language-model call at compression time, and scores 1,181 1{,}181 units per second where a dense encoder manages 103 103 and an LLM token-pruner 36 36 ( 11.5 × 11.5\times and 32.8 × 32.8\times slower respectively; Table 13 ). On agents at a 2048 2048 -token budget, LRE completes tasks in 19 steps where the compressor loops to 49 ( Figure 1 ) and reaches 41.1 % 41.1\% task success against full history’s 44.0 % 44.0\% while needing zero compressor calls ( Table 2 ). On conversational memory the scorer ranks evidence at 0.829 0.829 macro-AUC on LoCoMo and 0.708 0.708 on LongMemEval S without ever seeing the question, above dense ( 0.643 0.643 ) and token-pruning ( 0.402 0.402 ) encoders that each spend a forward pass ( Table 3 ). A natural question is that supervision for “relevance” requires expensive annotation. We show it does not: a self-supervised label derived from the system’s own later behavior recovers about 95 % 95\% of the supervised model’s signal beyond random ordering ( Table 4 ). The signal a deployed system needs to learn proactive retention, is already present in its logs. We present: • LRE, a learned query-blind eviction policy. We present a few kilobytes, CPU-only, language-model call-free scorer method that learns which units of history are load-bearing and keeps them by verbatim extraction, with one design serving both conversational memory and long-horizon agents. • Pareto efficiency in both domains. Under matched budgets, LRE is an efficient and cheaper baseline that preserves or exceeds performance gains. On agent tasks, it matches the success rate achieved by retaining the entire history, while reducing context token size by as much as ∼ 52 % {\sim}52\% (details in Appendix H ); on conversational memory, in retaining useful content, it outranks dense encoders without a forward pass of its own ( Table 3 ). • Fidelity, not just retrieval, is what eviction needs. A controlled study traces LRE’s agent advantage to verbatim fidelity: extraction keeps the load-bearing context a task needs in the future while compression or recency loses them, leaving fourteen tasks that could be solved by LRE alone ( Section 5.2 ). 2 Related Work Memory architectures for conversational and agentic LLMs. LLM memory systems decide both what to write to long-term store and what to keep active. MemGPT ( Packer et al., 2023 ) borrows virtual-memory paging to move content between context and external storage, while MemoryBank ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) folds both decisions into a time-based exponential decay model. On the write side, prior works have organised history into episodes, reflections, or linked notes that are periodically consolidated ( Park et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Chhikara et al., 2025 ; Nan et al., 2025 ) , and event-centric variants decompose dialogue into propositions to keep recall non-lossy ( Zhou and Han, 2025 ) . These mechanisms improve what is stored, but retention within a tier defaults to recency, decay, or a further LLM call. Reactive eviction under a fixed budget. A parallel line of work evicts directly from a size-capped buffer using cheap, query-blind signals. StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) retains a few initial attention-sink tokens alongside a recency window; H 2 O and SnapKV ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) keep the tokens that have received the most attention so far. They score a unit by how it has already been attended to rather than whether a later step may need it, and they operate on attention statistics at the token level inside a forward pass. Learned retention. Recent work learns what to keep rather than relying on attention heuristics. Selection-p ( Chung et al., 2024 ) learns self-supervised, task-agnostic token retention, and TRIM-KV ( Bui et al., 2025 ) learns a per-token retention gate at creation time that decays over the trajectory and evicts under a budget. Both confirm that learned retention can beat hand-designed decay. Their signal is produced inside the model, by forward passes or distilled gates tied to specific layers and heads, so each unit still costs a neural evaluation. We address whether such predictive principle holds for content units at zero added inference cost, with a scorer external to and independent of the generating model. LLM-based compression and its cost. At the expensive end, the model itself does the scoring. LLMLingua and LLMLingua-2 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) train a token classifier for compression rather than for any downstream task. In the agentic setting, context-management methods issue an LLM call to summarise or curate the accumulated history ( Kang et al., 2025 ) , adding latency on the critical path. Such summaries are typically conditioned on the current task, the query-aware advantage makes them a strong upper bound but not a deployable peer for a policy that can decide before the task context exists. Related directions. Adjacent work studies proactive computation prediction ( Pan et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) , systems-level context management ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) , and annotation-free supervision ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ; Izacard et al., 2021 ) ; we discuss these connections further in Appendix A . Along the cost axis, prior work spans zero neural cost (recency, MemoryBank, StreamingLLM), one neural pass per unit (dense and lexical salience, H 2 O, SnapKV, Selection-p, TRIM-KV), and one or more LLM calls per decision (LLMLingua, ACON, AgentFold). Along deployability, it splits into query-blind and query-aware scoring, and along timing, into reactive and proactive eviction. We therefore bridge that gap with a learned , query-blind , extractive scorer that anticipates which past content a future query will need, at zero added inference cost and independent of the host model, evaluated on both agentic ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) and conversational ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Maharana et al., 2024 ) memory with downstream gains. 3 Methodology 3.1 Framework: Score, Retain, Evict A long-running system holds a history H = [ u 1 , … , u t ] H=[u_{1},\dots,u_{t}] of units, where a unit is a dialogue turn or an agent action-observation step. AppWorld evaluates long-horizon agent execution under hidden-unit-test evaluation, while LoCoMo and LongMemEval S evaluate conversational memory retention under query-agnostic and multi-session settings respectively. Detailed benchmark descriptions, splits, labeling strategies, pseudocode and evaluation protocols are reported in Appendix B . 4.2 Baseline taxonomy We compare against a range of memory retention baselines, including simple heuristics (Recency / FIFO and exponential decay MemoryBank Zhong et al. (2024) ), content-based scoring (TF-IDF centroid salience), and dense embedding similarity methods (frozen BGE encoder Xiao et al. (2024) ) and LLMLingua-2 Pan et al. (2024) . For agentic evaluation, we compare against a no-compression upper bound, FIFO (First-In-First-Out) retention, and ACON (in-fork) Kang et al. (2025) . Across both agentic and conversational memory settings, no evaluated baseline is simultaneously more accurate and cheaper. LRE approaches full-history performance under a fixed budget, requires no compressor calls or neural inference, and can be trained from the system’s own later behavior without annotation. These results suggest that cheap learned relevance is sufficient for proactive retention. When future dependencies are weakly expressed or absent from the observed trajectory, the scorer can evict information that later becomes important. This limitation is inherent to proactive eviction and applies even with perfect training data. We evaluate on long-horizon agents and conversational memory, but not on multimodal memory, collaborative multi-agent systems, or environments with rapidly changing external state. The cost of mispredicting need is compute heavy: under recency or LRU, entries are discarded shortly before reuse and must be recomputed ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . This has motivated proactive systems. At the serving level, KVFlow and PBKV ( Pan et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) predict which agent or cache block will fire next from workflow structure and prefetch accordingly; at the agent level, AgentFold ( Ye et al., 2025 ) learns to fold and consolidate its own trajectory as it runs. These establish that anticipation beats reaction, but they anticipate computation from workflow graphs, or rewrite history through further LLM calls. We work along anticipating which past content an upcoming query will require, cheaply and without invoking an LLM. Systems-level context management. KV systems such as PagedAttention ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) remove memory fragmentation and enable cross-request reuse, raising throughput. Such caching lowers the cost of re-processing a seen context, but doesn’t relieve the cost of attending to that context, which becomes error-prone once critical content is buried within a long window ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Self-supervised relevance without labels. Training a scorer cheaply requires supervision that costs nothing to obtain. Hindsight relabeling ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ) reuses a failed trajectory by relabeling it with the goal it did reach for RL, and contrastive pretraining ( Izacard et al., 2021 ) learns dense retrievers with no relevance labels at all. We draw on this idea to derive retention labels directly from what later turns reused, at no annotation cost. (2024) serves as the primary benchmark for evaluating query-agnostic relevance prediction in conversational context eviction. The dataset contains 5,882 dialogue turns across 10 conversations, where each conversation forms a distinct evaluation group. 1. Data structure. Each sample corresponds to a dialogue turn u i u_{i} , and all turns within a conversation form a group g ∈ { 1 , … , 10 } g\in\{1,\dots,10\} . The task is to assign a relevance score to each turn without conditioning on a specific downstream query. About 24% of dialogue turns are considered truly relevant (gold evidence across questions) 2. Label construction. We consider two labeling regimes. In the supervised setting, a turn is labeled positive ( y i = 1 y_{i}=1 ) if it appears in the gold evidence set of any question associated with its conversation. Because these labels are pooled across all the questions tied to the conversation, it yields a query-agnostic relevance signal. The model learns to identify turns that are generally load-bearing or informative for the conversation, rather than those that just match a specific query. In the self-supervised setting, a turn is labeled positive if it shares at least 40% token overlap with an eventual answer for training without explicit annotations. The choice of token overlap percentile is discussed in Section D.1 3. Splitting and leakage-free training. We use a Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) protocol over the 10 conversations. In each fold, one full conversation is held out for evaluation while the remaining nine are used for training. To prevent information leakage, the vectorizer and StandardScaler are fitted strictly on training data within each fold. A deduplication guard removes any exact-text overlaps between training and test folds. Self-supervised labeling via quotation reuse. Since no human relevance annotations are available, we construct a zero-supervision label using a hindsight reuse criterion. During evaluation on test task splits, the agent operates in a ReAct-style loop. When the context length exceeds the token budget ( B = 2048 B=2048 ), the eviction module is triggered.
